questions.question: What does Fast Refresh do when you save a changed file during development?
options: Restarts the entire app from scratch every time
Metro recompiles just the changed module and hot-swaps it into the running app, generally preserving existing component state
It only works for changes to styling, not logic
It requires manually reloading the app each time
questions.explanation: Fast Refresh targets just the changed module for a quick in-place update, which is what makes the React Native dev loop fast compared to a full app restart on every change.

questions.question: When should you reach for Flipper instead of just React DevTools?
options: When you need to inspect something below the JS layer — native view hierarchy, raw network requests, native logs — not just the React component tree
Flipper is only used for iOS, DevTools only for Android
Flipper replaces the need for Metro entirely
questions.explanation: React DevTools shows the JS-level component tree and hooks state; Flipper adds native-level inspection (actual native views, network, native logs) on top of that.

questions.question: Why does clearing Metro's cache (`--reset-cache`) sometimes fix a 'stuck' bug that doesn't make sense?
options: It deletes the app from the device
It forces Metro to rebuild the JS bundle completely clean, eliminating stale cached modules that can otherwise linger after certain kinds of changes
It has no real effect and is just a superstition
It upgrades React Native to the latest version
questions.explanation: A stale cache can serve an outdated version of a module even after the source has changed; a clean rebuild removes that possibility.

questions.question: Why are source maps important when reading a React Native crash's stack trace?
options: They make the app run faster
Without them, you'd see a location in the minified/bundled JS output instead of the original source line in your actual file
Source maps are only relevant for CSS
They are required for Fast Refresh to work at all
questions.explanation: Source maps translate a crash location in the compiled bundle back to the corresponding line in your original source file, which is what makes the stack trace actually actionable.
